title: A garage bill: subtotal, tax and balance
source:
HILLSIDE TYRE & AUTO — 14 Old Harbour Road

INVOICE 4471

2 tyres, fitted ............... $18,500 each
Wheel alignment ............... $4,200
Labour ........................ $3,000

GCT is added to the subtotal at 15%.

A deposit of $10,000 has been paid on the card before the work started. The balance is due on collection.
prompt: Work through the invoice. Write every step of your method down — the figures alone will not show how you got them.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Work out the subtotal of the bill, before GCT is added. Show the working line by line.
parts.modelAnswer:
Tyres: 2 × $18,500 = $37,000
Add the alignment and the labour: $37,000 + $4,200 + $3,000
Subtotal = $44,200
markScheme: 1 mark for the tyres worked out as 2 × $18,500, with the working shown (not the answer alone).
1 mark for the correct tyres figure, $37,000.
1 mark for adding the alignment $4,200 and the labour $3,000 to the tyres total.
1 mark for the correct subtotal, $44,200, correctly labelled in dollars.
Up to 2 marks for a clear line-by-line method: a correct figure with no visible method cannot earn these.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: GCT is charged at 15% of the subtotal. Work out the GCT and the full amount of the bill.
markScheme: 1 mark for finding 10% of the correct subtotal ($4,420) by a stated method.
1 mark for building 15% from 10% + 5% (accept any correct method, including 0.15 × subtotal).
1 mark for the correct GCT, $6,630.
1 mark for adding the GCT to the subtotal rather than subtracting it.
1 mark for the correct full bill, $50,830, in dollars.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The customer has already paid a deposit of $10,000. Work out the balance still due, and check that your answer is sensible.
parts.modelAnswer:
Balance = $50,830 − $10,000 = $40,830
The deposit is a small part of a bill of about $50,000, so the balance should still be close to $50,000. $40,830 agrees, and it is smaller than the bill, as a balance must be.
markScheme: 1 mark for subtracting the deposit from the full bill.
1 mark for the correct balance, $40,830.
1 mark for keeping the unit ($) with the answer.
1 mark for a written check that the balance is smaller than the bill and close to the estimate.

title: A garden job: fencing, turfed area and cost
source:
JOB NOTE — plot at Lot 8, Innswood

The plot is rectangular, 24 m long and 15 m wide.

A straight path runs along one of the SHORT sides. The path is 15 m long and 1.2 m wide and will be paved.

Everything else on the plot is to be turfed.

A fence is to run all the way round the plot, except for a gate opening 2 m wide.

Prices: turf $1,250 per square metre; paving $2,400 per square metre; fencing $1,850 per metre.
prompt: Answer all three parts. Name the quantity you are working out before you calculate it, and keep the units with every figure.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Work out the length of fencing needed. State clearly which quantity you are using and why.
parts.modelAnswer:
Fencing runs round the outside, so this is a perimeter question, not an area one.
Perimeter of the rectangle = 2 × (24 + 15) = 2 × 39 = 78 m
The gate opening is not fenced, so take it off: 78 − 2 = 76 m of fencing.
markScheme: 1 mark for naming the quantity as perimeter (distance round the outside) rather than area.
1 mark for adding the length and the width (24 + 15 = 39).
1 mark for doubling, because each length appears twice.
1 mark for the correct perimeter, 78 m, in metres.
1 mark for subtracting the 2 m gate opening.
1 mark for the correct fencing length, 76 m.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Work out the area that will be turfed. Show each area you calculate.
parts.modelAnswer:
Whole plot: 24 × 15 = 360 m²
Path: 15 × 1.2 = 18 m²
The turfed area is everything except the path: 360 − 18 = 342 m²
markScheme: 1 mark for the area of the whole plot, 360 m², with the multiplication shown.
1 mark for the area of the path, 18 m².
1 mark for subtracting the path from the plot rather than adding it.
1 mark for the correct turfed area, 342 m².
1 mark for the answer in square metres, not metres.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Work out the cost of the turf. Check that your answer is the right size for the job.
parts.modelAnswer:
Cost = 342 × $1,250 = $427,500
342 m² is a bit more than a third of a thousand square metres, and each square metre costs about $1,250, so the cost should be a few hundred thousand dollars, not a few thousand. $427,500 agrees.
markScheme: 1 mark for multiplying the turfed area by the price per square metre.
1 mark for the correct cost, $427,500.
1 mark for keeping the units sensible (square metres × dollars per square metre = dollars).
1 mark for a written check on the size of the answer.

title: Six days of takings: mean, median and what to report
source:
TAKINGS FOR THE WEEK — SNACK STOP, MAY PEN

Mon ...... $12,000
Tue ...... $9,000
Wed ...... $15,000
Thu ...... $12,000
Fri ...... $18,000
Sat ...... $12,000

Sunday: the shop is closed.
prompt: Use the six days of takings. In part (c), write your answer as a short paragraph that names the figures you are relying on.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Work out the mean of the six days' takings. Show the total before you divide.
markScheme: 1 mark for adding all six values, with the addition shown.
1 mark for the correct total, $78,000.
1 mark for dividing by 6 — the number of values, not the number of different values.
1 mark for the correct mean, $13,000.
1 mark for the unit ($) with the answer.
1 mark for showing the division as a step rather than only the final figure.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the median and the mode of the six days. Put the values in order first and show that order.
parts.modelAnswer:
In order: 9,000  12,000  12,000  12,000  15,000  18,000
There are six values, so the median is the mean of the third and fourth:
(12,000 + 12,000) ÷ 2 = $12,000
The mode is the value that occurs most often: $12,000 (it appears three times).
markScheme: 1 mark for writing the values in order before reading anything off.
1 mark for recognising that six values give an even middle, so the median is the mean of the two middle values.
1 mark for the correct median, $12,000.
1 mark for the correct mode, $12,000, with the reason (it occurs three times).
1 mark for noticing that two different averages give the same figure here and saying so.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The owner wants one sentence telling a new supplier how a typical day goes. Which average would you use, and why? Refer to the figures.
parts.modelAnswer: A typical day is about $12,000, so I would report the median or the mode rather than the mean. The mean is $13,000, which is pulled upward by Friday's $18,000 — a figure only one day reached. Five of the six days were at or below $12,000, so $12,000 is the figure that honestly describes a normal day.
markScheme: 1 mark for choosing the median or the mode, not the mean.
1 mark for explaining that the mean is lifted by the one high day ($18,000).
1 mark for referring to the actual figures (five of six days at or below $12,000).
1 mark for writing it as one clear sentence, in the form the question asked for.

title: A paint mix and a plan: ratio, scale and value
source:
DECORATING NOTE

Mix the colour with white in the ratio 1 : 4 (one part colour to four parts white).

A plan of the room is drawn at a scale of 1 : 50.

Paint is sold in two tins: 5 litres for $3,600, and 2 litres for $1,500.
prompt: Answer all three parts. Say which operation the situation calls for before you calculate, and keep the units with each figure.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The decorator uses 15 litres of white paint. Work out how much colour is needed to keep the mix correct.
parts.modelAnswer:
The ratio says 4 parts white go with 1 part colour, so the white is the larger quantity and the colour is one quarter of it.
Colour = 15 ÷ 4 = 3.75 litres
Check: 3.75 × 4 = 15, so the ratio 3.75 : 15 simplifies to 1 : 4 ✓
markScheme: 1 mark for identifying 4 parts white against 1 part colour and stating which is larger.
1 mark for dividing the white by 4 rather than multiplying.
1 mark for the correct amount, 3.75 litres.
1 mark for keeping the unit (litres).
Up to 2 marks for the check: showing that 3.75 × 4 returns to 15, or that the ratio simplifies correctly.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: On the plan, a wall measures 9.6 cm. Work out the real length of the wall in metres.
parts.modelAnswer:
Scale 1 : 50 means each 1 cm on the plan is 50 cm in real life.
9.6 × 50 = 480 cm
480 ÷ 100 = 4.8 m
markScheme: 1 mark for multiplying the plan length by the scale factor 50 (not dividing).
1 mark for the correct length in centimetres, 480 cm.
1 mark for converting to metres by dividing by 100.
1 mark for the correct answer, 4.8 m, in metres as asked.
1 mark for a sensible check: a room wall should come out a few metres, not a few centimetres.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Which tin is the better value? Work out the price per litre for each and compare them.
parts.modelAnswer:
5-litre tin: $3,600 ÷ 5 = $720 per litre
2-litre tin: $1,500 ÷ 2 = $750 per litre
$720 is less than $750, so the 5-litre tin is the better value.
markScheme: 1 mark for dividing each price by its number of litres, both tins.
1 mark for the correct unit prices, $720 and $750 per litre.
1 mark for comparing them and naming the cheaper per litre.
1 mark for answering the question asked (which is better value), not just giving two figures.

title: A water tank: volume, capacity and the cost to fill
source:
TANK FITTING NOTE

Tank measurements: 120 cm long, 80 cm wide, 75 cm high.

The tank is filled with a bucket that holds 15 litres.

Water is charged at $95 for every 1,000 litres.
prompt: Answer all three parts. Convert between cubic centimetres and litres deliberately, and show where you do it.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Work out the volume of the tank in cubic centimetres, then state its capacity in litres.
parts.modelAnswer:
Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height, all in the same unit (centimetres here).
120 × 80 = 9,600
9,600 × 75 = 720,000 cm³
One cubic centimetre holds one millilitre, so 720,000 cm³ = 720,000 ml.
One litre is 1,000 ml: 720,000 ÷ 1,000 = 720 litres.
markScheme: 1 mark for multiplying length × width × height rather than adding them.
1 mark for the correct volume, 720,000 cm³, with the unit.
1 mark for showing the intermediate step (9,600 cm² × 75).
1 mark for using 1 cm³ = 1 ml.
1 mark for converting to litres by dividing by 1,000.
1 mark for the correct capacity, 720 litres.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: How many full buckets of 15 litres are needed to fill the tank? Show the division.
parts.modelAnswer:
The tank holds 720 litres and one bucket holds 15 litres.
720 ÷ 15 = 48 buckets
Check: 48 × 15 = 720 ✓
markScheme: 1 mark for dividing the capacity by the bucket size, not multiplying.
1 mark for the correct answer, 48 buckets.
1 mark for showing the division as a step.
1 mark for multiplying back to check (48 × 15 = 720).
1 mark for a whole-number answer that is labelled in buckets.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Work out the cost of the water needed to fill the tank once. Round to the nearest cent if you need to.
parts.modelAnswer:
Water costs $95 per 1,000 litres.
720 litres = 720 ÷ 1,000 = 0.72 thousand litres
Cost = 0.72 × $95 = $68.40
markScheme: 1 mark for working out how many thousands of litres are involved (0.72).
1 mark for multiplying by the price per 1,000 litres.
1 mark for the correct cost, $68.40, in dollars and cents.
1 mark for a sensible check: 720 litres is less than a thousand, so the cost must be less than $95.

title: Egg production: a percentage change and a claim
source:
EGGS COLLECTED, WEEK BY WEEK — HILLVIEW SMALL FARM

Week 1 ...... 240
Week 2 ...... 264
Week 3 ...... 288
Week 4 ...... 336
prompt: Use the four weekly figures. In parts (b) and (c), write your answer as a short explanation that names the figures you are relying on.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Work out the percentage increase from week 1 to week 2. Show the increase before you compare it.
parts.modelAnswer:
Increase = 264 − 240 = 24 eggs
The percentage is the increase compared with the STARTING figure:
24 ÷ 240 = 0.1
0.1 × 100 = 10%
markScheme: 1 mark for finding the increase, 24, before any percentage is written.
1 mark for comparing the increase with the starting figure (240), not with the later figure.
1 mark for the correct division, 24 ÷ 240 = 0.1.
1 mark for converting to a percentage by multiplying by 100.
1 mark for the correct answer, 10%.
1 mark for keeping the working visible rather than only the percentage.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A customer says: 'Production is rising, so it will double by week 8.' Using the four weeks of figures, say what the data does and does not support.
parts.modelAnswer: The data supports the first half: production rose every week — 240, 264, 288, 336 — so it is rising across these four weeks. It does not support the prediction. Four weeks cannot show what happens by week 8, and the size of each rise is not steady: the rises were 24, 24 and then 48, so there is no fixed rule to carry forward. A doubling by week 8 would need figures nobody has collected.
markScheme: 1 mark for saying the data supports a rise across the four weeks, quoting some of the figures.
1 mark for identifying the size of the weekly rises (24, 24, 48) and noting they are not constant.
1 mark for explaining that a prediction for week 8 needs data that does not exist yet.
1 mark for separating what is supported from what is not, rather than dismissing the whole statement.
1 mark for writing the answer as an explanation that names the figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Name one further piece of information that would make a forecast for week 8 more trustworthy, and say why it would help.
parts.modelAnswer: The same figures for the same weeks in a previous year. If production peaks and then falls at this time of year, a rise carried forward to week 8 would be misleading; if last year's weeks 5 to 8 continued rising by a similar amount, the forecast would have some backing. Any of the following is accepted on the same reasoning: figures for weeks 5 onwards as they happen, the number of hens laying, or the feed and weather records for those weeks.
markScheme: 1 mark for naming a specific, collectable piece of information (last year's figures for the same weeks, later weeks as they arrive, flock size, feed or weather records).
1 mark for saying how it would be used — comparing like with like, or turning an assumption into evidence.
1 mark for keeping the answer tied to this farm's figures rather than a general statement about data.
1 mark for writing it in the form asked for: one item of information, with the reason.
